title: Trump Pardoned Peter Y. Atkinson, Convicted of Three Mail-Fraud Counts
description_short: The DOJ clemency list records Trump’s pardon of Peter Y. Atkinson and identifies three mail-fraud counts in the Northern District of Illinois.
description_medium: The Justice Department’s clemency list records a Trump pardon for Peter Y. Atkinson and identifies three mail-fraud counts in the Northern District of Illinois. It lists 345 days already served, three years of supervised release and a $3,000 fine, amended in 2011. The official entry supports the grant and case details but gives no rationale or evidence of favoritism, exchange or another corrupt act.
description_long: The Justice Department’s clemency list records President Donald Trump’s pardon of Peter Y. Atkinson in a Northern District of Illinois case involving three mail-fraud counts. It lists a sentence of 345 days already served, three years of supervised release and a $3,000 fine, and notes a 2011 sentence amendment. National Post reported that Atkinson was a former Hollinger vice president and that he and John Boultbee were convicted of fraud alongside company founder Conrad Black. The report described bonuses paid from Hollinger International earnings and quoted the White House citing Lord Black’s support for the pardons. Black had separately received a Trump pardon in 2019. The Justice Department list does not explain why Trump selected Atkinson. The cited records do not establish a contribution-linked favor, personal exchange or improper motive. A pardon grants executive clemency; it does not erase the underlying conviction or establish innocence.

The signed clemency warrant states that President Donald Trump commuted Ashley’s prison sentence to time already served, or to zero days if no prison time had been served. title: Trump Administration Proposed Ending NASA’s OCO-2 and OCO-3 Missions
description_short: The Trump administration’s FY2026 budget request proposed ending NASA’s OCO-2 and OCO-3 missions.
description_medium: An August 2025 Associated Press report said the Trump administration’s FY2026 budget request included no funding for NASA’s Orbiting Carbon Observatory missions, OCO-2 and OCO-3. NASA told AP the missions were beyond their prime mission and were being terminated to align with the president’s budget priorities. The reporting described a proposed end to operations, not physical destruction or a completed shutdown.
description_long: On August 6, 2025, the Associated Press reported that the Trump administration’s FY2026 presidential budget request included no funding for NASA’s Orbiting Carbon Observatory missions, OCO-2 and OCO-3. The satellites monitor atmospheric carbon dioxide and plant health. NASA told AP the missions were beyond their prime mission and were being terminated to align with the president’s agenda and budget priorities. The report described a budget proposal and planned termination; it did not establish that the satellites had already been shut down or physically destroyed. An unfunded request can signal an administration’s priorities and affect agency planning, but the AP report did not describe Congress’s final funding decision or give a completed shutdown date. NASA’s explanation linked the proposed termination to the missions being beyond their prime phase and to the administration’s budget priorities. The report concerns plans for the two observatories, not a realized destruction of either spacecraft.

title: Mueller Report Says Trump Directed McGahn to Seek the Special Counsel’s Removal
description_short: The Mueller report says Trump directed McGahn to tell the acting attorney general Mueller should be removed.
description_medium: The Justice Department’s Mueller report says Trump called White House counsel Don McGahn on June 17, 2017, and directed him to tell the acting attorney general that Robert Mueller had conflicts and must be removed. McGahn did not carry out the direction, deciding he would resign rather than trigger what he viewed as a potential “Saturday Night Massacre.”
description_long: Volume II of the Justice Department’s Mueller report recounts a June 17, 2017 call in which President Donald Trump directed White House counsel Don McGahn to contact Acting Attorney General Rod Rosenstein and say that Special Counsel Robert Mueller had conflicts of interest and must be removed. The report says McGahn did not contact Rosenstein to deliver the demand. He instead told senior White House officials about the call and decided he would resign rather than take a step he viewed as a potential “Saturday Night Massacre.” The report also recounts that, after news stories described the episode in January 2018, Trump asked McGahn to deny that Trump had ordered Mueller’s removal. McGahn declined to issue a denial. The report documents a direction and McGahn’s response; it does not say Mueller was removed in this episode. Mueller remained special counsel.
